title: Python: controlled asynchronous work
command:
import asyncio

async def observe(value, gate):
    async with gate:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        return value * 2

async def main():
    gate = asyncio.Semaphore(2)
    print(await asyncio.gather(*(observe(x, gate) for x in range(4))))

asyncio.run(main())
explanation: Learn bounded concurrent waiting using a synthetic task.
options: At most two tasks enter the guarded section together. This is not a requests-per-second limiter and does not automatically speed up CPU-heavy computation.

explanation: A baseline makes discovery results interpretable. Compare a known resource with a deliberately absent one.

title: Inspect redirects before following them
explanation: A directory without its trailing slash normally redirects to the slash path in this server.
options: -I sends HEAD. Inspect Location; on real applications verify its destination is in scope before following. HEAD can behave differently from GET.

explanation: Keep response headers separate from the body so later comparisons have clear inputs.

title: Vulnerability, exposure, exploit and risk
command: A public login page is exposure. Missing authorization that reveals another test user invoice is a vulnerability.
explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness that can violate a security requirement. Exposure makes a component reachable; an exploit takes advantage of a weakness. Risk combines likelihood and consequences in a particular environment.
impact_detail: Impact concerns confidentiality, integrity or availability, including business effects.
lab_check: Write the intended security rule first, then compare a permitted and a prohibited action using synthetic data.
options: Define security requirements and trust boundaries before choosing controls. Prioritize by affected assets, exploit conditions and realistic business impact.
result: Document what is fixed, what was actually tested and what remains uncertain.
pitfall: An open port, HTTP 500, outdated-looking banner or scanner severity is not sufficient proof.

title: Broken authentication
command: A training account is treated as fully logged in before its required second factor finishes.
explanation: The application incorrectly establishes who a requester is, or permits an incomplete authentication flow to count as complete.
impact_detail: An unintended user may obtain account access.
lab_check: Use a dedicated lab account and check transitions between logged-out, password-verified and fully authenticated states.
options: Use established authentication components, enforce MFA server-side, protect recovery paths and throttle repeated failures with a considered lockout policy.
result: Confirm incomplete authentication cannot reach protected actions and valid login still works.
pitfall: Authorization is a separate decision even after identity is correctly established.

title: Broken access control: IDOR and BOLA
command: User A requests a synthetic invoice belonging only to User B and receives its contents.
explanation: A server trusts an object identifier without verifying the requester right to that object. IDOR commonly describes direct-reference cases; BOLA emphasizes object authorization in APIs.
impact_detail: Cross-account reading, changes or deletion may become possible.
lab_check: Create two lab users and separate synthetic objects. Compare the same read using each identity.
options: Check subject, action, object and tenant permissions on the server for every relevant request; deny unspecified access.
result: Other-user access fails without exposing data; legitimate owner access succeeds.
pitfall: Random IDs reduce guessing but do not replace permission checks.

title: Session fixation and invalidation
command: A copied training session still reads a private page after explicit logout.
explanation: Session identifiers remain valid across unsafe transitions or continue authorizing requests after intended termination.
impact_detail: Someone holding the identifier can continue acting as the user.
lab_check: Record a lab session before login, after login and after logout. Compare server authorization, not only browser cookie disappearance.
options: Generate unpredictable identifiers, rotate after privilege changes, enforce server-side expiration and invalidate sessions appropriately. Set suitable Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes.
result: Old sessions fail after termination and rotation; the new valid session succeeds.
pitfall: HttpOnly prevents script access to cookies, not every action an injected script could perform.

title: Password reset and recovery flaws
command: A synthetic recovery token remains reusable after a successful password reset.
explanation: Recovery grants account control without adequately binding the proof to the account, action and expiry window.
impact_detail: Account takeover or denial of access to the legitimate owner.
lab_check: Use only a lab inbox. Check expiry, single use, account binding and handling of previously issued tokens.
options: Use high-entropy single-use tokens, short justified validity, uniform responses and trusted reset-link origins. Notify the owner of relevant changes.
result: Used, expired and mismatched tokens fail; one valid token completes the intended flow.
pitfall: A visually identical response does not ensure timing and side effects reveal no account existence.

title: JWT validation failures
command: A training API accepts a well-formed token issued for a different service.
explanation: An application trusts token claims without correctly validating cryptographic integrity and the intended token context.
impact_detail: False identity or excessive permissions may be accepted.
lab_check: Review issuer, audience, expiry and signature checks using tokens from your test issuer and separate lab services.
options: Pin allowed algorithms and trusted key sources; validate signature, issuer, audience and time claims. Keep authorization checks separate from token parsing.
result: Wrong audience, issuer, signature and expired tokens fail; the intended token works.
pitfall: Base64 decoding is not signature validation; signing is not encryption.

title: OAuth and OpenID Connect mistakes
command: A lab client accepts a response created for a different login transaction.
explanation: Login or delegated authorization loses the binding between browser session, authorization response, client and redirect destination.
impact_detail: Login confusion, account linking errors or token disclosure.
lab_check: Use dedicated test clients and accounts. Trace the intended issuer, redirect URI and transaction correlation across the complete flow.
options: Use a maintained library, exact redirect registration, PKCE where applicable and correct state/nonce protections for the chosen flow. Validate issuer and audience.
result: Mismatched transactions and destinations are rejected while the normal flow remains usable.
pitfall: OAuth delegates access; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer. An access token is not automatically an ID token.

title: Tenant and function isolation
command: A basic training user can call an admin-only export endpoint, or switch to another test tenant.
explanation: The server enforces login but omits the tenant boundary or permission needed for a privileged function.
impact_detail: Cross-organization data exposure or unauthorized administration.
lab_check: Define tenant, role, action and object combinations; test a small allowed/denied matrix using synthetic records.
options: Derive tenant context from trusted identity, enforce function permissions and scope all data access consistently.
result: Cross-tenant and privileged requests fail; correct tenant and role operations succeed.
pitfall: Hiding menu items only changes the interface; it does not secure the endpoint.

title: SQL injection
command: A search feature assembles query text directly from the supplied search string.
explanation: User-controlled text changes SQL structure instead of remaining a bound data value.
impact_detail: Unauthorized database reads or writes; further effects depend on database privileges and configuration.
lab_check: In a dedicated vulnerable lab, trace data into query construction and compare controlled valid/invalid input with server-side evidence.
options: Use parameterized queries; allowlist identifiers that cannot be bound. Limit database permissions and avoid detailed database errors in responses.
result: Special characters are processed as data, normal searches work and query structure stays fixed.
pitfall: An ORM can still be unsafe when using concatenated raw SQL. An error alone does not prove injection.

title: XSS: reflected, stored and DOM-based
command: A lab comment is inserted into an HTML execution context instead of rendered as text.
explanation: Untrusted content reaches an executable browser context. Reflected input returns in a response, stored input persists, and DOM-based XSS involves unsafe client-side processing.
impact_detail: Actions or data access in the affected origin, depending on user privileges and browser controls.
lab_check: Trace a harmless unique marker from input to its output context in a dedicated lab. Confirm unsafe interpretation separately from simple reflection.
options: Use context-appropriate encoding, safe text DOM APIs and maintained sanitization when HTML is required. Use CSP as an additional layer.
result: Special text stays inert in each relevant context and legitimate formatting remains correct.
pitfall: One escaping method does not cover HTML, JavaScript, CSS and URL contexts.

title: NoSQL injection
command: An endpoint expecting a text value accepts a nested object that changes matching behavior.
explanation: Untrusted request structures or operators become part of a database filter without type and schema constraints.
impact_detail: Unexpected record selection or authentication/authorization failures.
lab_check: Use a lab database with synthetic records; inspect how unexpected input types reach query construction.
options: Enforce schemas and expected scalar types, build server-controlled filters and avoid accepting arbitrary query operators.
result: Objects and unexpected operators are rejected; supported scalar values return only intended records.
pitfall: Changing databases does not remove injection risks; syntax and entry points change.

title: OS command and argument injection
command: A diagnostic feature joins user text into a command string.
explanation: Input changes a spawned program invocation or shell command instead of being constrained data.
impact_detail: Commands may run with the application service privileges.
lab_check: Review the invocation path in a disposable lab; use inert inputs and process logs to see whether argument boundaries are preserved.
options: Prefer a direct library API. If execution is required, avoid the shell, use explicit argument arrays and strictly validate permitted values and options.
result: Inputs cannot add command structure or unintended flags; normal supported operations still work.
pitfall: Avoiding the shell reduces risk but does not stop unsafe options interpreted by the called program.

title: Cross-site request forgery: CSRF
command: A lab profile change accepts a request without the required anti-CSRF proof.
explanation: A browser sends an unwanted state-changing request using credentials it attaches automatically, and the server lacks an adequate intent check.
impact_detail: Unwanted account or business-state changes as the signed-in user.
lab_check: Use a reversible synthetic preference in a lab. Check absent, invalid and mismatched tokens and the relevant browser context.
options: Use framework CSRF protection, appropriate origin validation and SameSite settings. Require suitable confirmation for high-impact actions.
result: Invalid cross-site attempts fail; valid intended changes still succeed.
pitfall: CORS controls response reading, not all request sending. State changes should not rely on GET.

title: CORS misconfiguration
command: A private lab API reflects an arbitrary Origin and permits credentialed reading.
explanation: An application allows an unintended browser origin to read sensitive responses across origins.
impact_detail: Sensitive response data can become accessible to a different site under the necessary browser conditions.
lab_check: Use two controlled lab origins and synthetic data. Observe whether the browser actually exposes the response to script.
options: Allow only exact trusted origins where sharing is needed; minimize credentialed sharing and vary cached responses correctly.
result: Disallowed origins cannot read private responses; approved clients still work.
pitfall: A wildcard on public data is not automatically vulnerable. Wildcard origin does not enable credentialed reads in compliant browsers.

title: Unrestricted file upload
command: A lab upload is served as active content where only inert documents were intended.
explanation: Uploaded content or metadata is trusted beyond its intended purpose, storage location or permissions.
impact_detail: Stored browser attacks, unsafe processing, resource exhaustion or server execution in some deployments.
lab_check: Use inert files in a dedicated lab; examine type checks, naming, retrieval permissions and storage location.
options: Allowlist necessary formats, check content, generate safe names, limit sizes and store outside executable paths. Apply per-object access controls and safe processing.
result: Disallowed content and oversized files fail; approved uploads remain retrievable only by permitted users.
pitfall: Extensions and browser-supplied MIME types alone do not establish file safety.

title: Path traversal and file inclusion
command: A training download feature resolves a path beyond its designated fixture directory.
explanation: Untrusted path input escapes an allowed directory or selects content outside the intended resource set. Inclusion can additionally interpret selected content.
impact_detail: Unintended file disclosure, modification or execution depending on the operation.
lab_check: Create harmless fixture files inside and outside a lab root and verify only the authorized fixture is accessible.
options: Prefer server-side resource IDs. Resolve and validate the final path against the allowed root, consider symlinks and enforce permissions.
result: Outside-root and unauthorized resources fail; legitimate files still work.
pitfall: Removing one traversal string is insufficient; normalization and platform behavior matter.

title: Server-side template injection
command: A preview feature compiles a user-written message as a template.
explanation: User content becomes template source evaluated by the server rather than a variable rendered by a fixed template.
impact_detail: Data disclosure or server-side execution, depending on the engine and available objects.
lab_check: In an isolated template lab, distinguish literal text from evaluation with a harmless calculation and code-path review.
options: Keep template source trusted and fixed. Pass untrusted content as data; constrain available functionality if user templating is a required product feature.
result: Template-like input remains literal where expected and approved formatting still works.
pitfall: Client-side template behavior and server-side evaluation have different trust boundaries.

title: Server-side request forgery: SSRF
command: An image import feature fetches a controlled lab endpoint outside its allowed destination set.
explanation: A user influences requests made by the application server beyond the intended destination or protocol.
impact_detail: Unintended access from the server network position or disclosure of server-side response data.
lab_check: Use an endpoint you control with synthetic markers. Confirm requests in server logs without contacting sensitive infrastructure.
options: Constrain protocols and destinations, validate resolved addresses and redirects, and enforce outbound network policy.
result: Disallowed destinations fail through all redirect paths; valid imports still work.
pitfall: Browser access restrictions do not constrain what a server can request.

title: XML external entities: XXE
command: A lab parser unexpectedly attempts to load an external fixture during document parsing.
explanation: An XML parser resolves external entities or other external resources when processing untrusted XML.
impact_detail: File exposure, server-side requests or resource consumption under permissive parser settings.
lab_check: Use controlled fixtures and parser instrumentation in an isolated lab; review the exact parser and configuration.
options: Disable unnecessary DTD and external-entity processing and external resource access; use maintained parsers and input/resource limits.
result: The intended XML schema works while external resource resolution is blocked.
pitfall: A setting that secures one parser API may not secure a separate library or processing pipeline.

title: Unsafe deserialization
command: An application restores client-supplied objects instead of parsing a constrained data schema.
explanation: Untrusted serialized input recreates complex objects or invokes behavior that was not intended for external control.
impact_detail: State manipulation or execution depending on available object behavior and libraries.
lab_check: Inspect the deserialization boundary in a disposable lab using benign records and unexpected type tests.
options: Use constrained data formats and schemas, avoid untrusted native-object deserialization and limit allowed types where unavoidable.
result: Unexpected types fail without side effects while legitimate data remains compatible.
pitfall: An encoded blob is not automatically encrypted or trustworthy. Integrity checks do not fix every unsafe object design.

title: Start Burp Suite
explanation: Launch the Kali-packaged Burp desktop application.
options: Use a temporary project for the first exercise. Save features differ by edition; do not assume every Community workflow persists between launches.

Proxy > Open browser
Visit http://127.0.0.1:8877/
Keep interception off while browsing initially.
explanation: The embedded browser simplifies proxy setup for the first local exercise.
options: Use the practice service from the foundations chapter. Browser traffic can include unrelated requests; verify host and port before sending any request again.

command:
Find http://127.0.0.1:8877 in Target / Site map.
Add this exact origin to scope.
Filter HTTP history to in-scope traffic.
explanation: Scope keeps investigation focused on the exercise.

Proxy > HTTP history
Select GET / on port 8877.
Inspect the request and response panels.
explanation: History records what actually traveled through the proxy.

Turn Intercept on.
Refresh the local page.
Inspect the paused GET, then Forward it.
Turn Intercept off.

title: Compare paths in Repeater
command:
Send the local GET request to Repeater.
Send GET /.
Change only the path to /missing-page.
Send again and compare.
explanation: Repeater lets you change one variable and inspect the response.
options: Keep host and port fixed. Save notes describing the baseline and changed request, so a difference is attributable to your edit.
result: 200 for / and 404 for the missing path.

title: Understand encoding with Decoder
command:
Open Decoder.
Enter: hello%20lab
Decode as URL encoding.
Compare with the original text.
explanation: Encoding represents characters; it does not provide secrecy.
options: The decoded result is hello lab. Encode once for the intended protocol layer; repeated decoding may change meaning. Never paste real access tokens into online decoders.

title: Compare response evidence
command:
Send baseline and changed responses to Comparer.
Choose a word or byte comparison.
Review status, headers and body changes.
explanation: Differential testing helps isolate meaningful behavior.
options: Timestamps, request IDs and anti-CSRF values may vary normally. Annotate these differences before concluding that an access-control or injection issue exists.
result: A comparison with meaningful and incidental differences separated.

title: Run a three-value Intruder exercise
command:
Send the local GET / request to Intruder.
Clear automatic positions.
Mark only the path segment after /.
Use simple payloads: help/, robots.txt, missing-page.
Use one concurrent request and run once.
explanation: Use the three known paths to learn payload positions and response tables.
options: Keep the attack to one position and three values. Community throughput and controls differ from Professional. This is content comparison, not password guessing.
result: Three candidate-path results plus any tool housekeeping requests.

title: Plan authenticated testing
command:
Create two lab identities with different roles.
Record login and logout behavior.
Confirm which cookie or token identifies each account.
Repeat one harmless account-specific read as each user.
explanation: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides what that identity may access.
options: Use a deliberately configured training app. Keep cookie jars separate, verify the active user, and refresh expired sessions. A login redirect can masquerade as a negative security result.
result: Evidence linked to the correct account and role.

title: Use Scanner with explicit limits
command:
Professional edition: select a scoped training request.
Review the scan configuration and insertion points.
Choose the smallest relevant audit.
Review generated traffic and manually validate each alert.
explanation: Burp automated Scanner is a Professional feature. Community users can follow manual proxy and Repeater exercises.
options: Active auditing sends extra requests and can change application state. A clean result has limited coverage; an alert needs reproduction and context.
result: A bounded audit with reviewed evidence.

title: Evaluate extensions and session automation
command:
Record a task the built-in tools cannot handle.
Review an extension source, permissions and network behavior.
Try it in a disposable project with synthetic data.
For session rules, test on one request before wider use.
explanation: Extensions execute code; session handling can alter many requests automatically.
options: Check that tokens are inserted only for intended hosts. Avoid installing extensions merely because they are popular; keep a reproducible record of versions and settings.
result: A controlled extension or session-handling decision.

title: Gobuster: discover the three practice paths
explanation: Gobuster tries candidate paths from a wordlist. Start the practice server first.
options: dir selects paths; -u sets the URL; -w supplies words. One thread and a per-thread delay keep this exercise small.
result: help redirects, robots.txt exists, and the missing path is normally excluded.

title: DirBuster: launch the graphical tool
explanation: DirBuster provides a graphical interface for wordlist-based path discovery.
options: Kali provides the Java application. Use local help if launch fails. Its interface and controls differ from Gobuster despite the similar purpose.

title: Wappalyzer: read technology fingerprints
command:
Install the official Wappalyzer browser extension in a lab profile.
Visit an authorized application.
Open the extension panel and record detected technologies.
explanation: Wappalyzer infers technologies from observable page and response signals.
options: Results can be incomplete or mistaken. Review extension permissions. Avoid testing a private authenticated application through an external lookup service without understanding data sharing.

title: Subfinder: inspect available sources
explanation: Subfinder collects names from passive sources such as public datasets and provider APIs.
options: -ls lists sources. Provider credentials and availability affect coverage. Passive enumeration still sends queries to third-party services.

title: ffuf: discover paths with a marker
explanation: ffuf replaces FUZZ with each line of the wordlist.
options: -t controls concurrency; -rate caps requests per second; -mc all initially shows all status codes so the negative baseline remains visible.
result: Results including the known missing path.

title: ZAP: begin with manual exploration
command:
Start ZAP and choose a temporary session.
Use Manual Explore with http://127.0.0.1:8877/.
Browse the local page and help link.
Inspect history and passive alerts.
explanation: ZAP is another intercepting proxy and assessment platform.
options: Use a different listener port if Burp already occupies 8080. Passive analysis examines proxied messages; spidering and active scanning generate additional traffic.
result: Traffic history and any passive observations.

title: Gobuster: try selected file extensions
explanation: Extension expansion adds requests for each candidate.
options: Estimate request count before using a larger list. Words that already contain an extension may produce unhelpful combinations. Review local help for version differences.
result: Mostly missing variants on this deliberately small site.

title: DirBuster: configure a small path search
command:
Target: http://127.0.0.1:8877/
Wordlist: ~/kali-lab/web-practice/words.txt (browse to the full path)

Start; review results; stop when the small list finishes.
explanation: Use the same tiny lab to compare graphical and terminal discovery.
options: Review directory/file mode and extensions because they change request count. A 403 response does not prove sensitive data is retrievable. Save the result and settings together.
result: A small path inventory comparable with Gobuster.

title: Subfinder: query an owned domain
explanation: Run only after choosing a domain you own or have permission to assess.
options: -d supplies the domain; -silent reduces output; -o writes the result. Stop if the input is empty or not your approved domain. Provider limits and missing keys may reduce results.
result: Candidate names; no guarantee that each currently resolves.

title: ffuf: filter after measuring a baseline
explanation: Filtering removes expected negative responses from the result view.
options: -fc 404 fits this static lab. For a soft-404 application, inspect response size, words and content before choosing a filter. Overbroad filtering can hide real endpoints.
result: Existing or redirecting paths; 404 results hidden.

title: ProjectDiscovery httpx: inspect one service
explanation: ProjectDiscovery httpx summarizes HTTP endpoints. It is different from the Python HTTPX library.
options: Confirm httpx -h identifies the intended product. -sc shows status, -title the page title, -cl length; -nfs keeps the input scheme.
result: A compact summary of the practice service.

title: Katana: crawl local links
explanation: Katana follows links rather than guessing every possible path.
options: -d limits depth; -c and -p limit concurrency; -rl limits rate; -cs limits crawl scope. Review extracted URLs before treating them as authorized targets.
result: The linked help route may be discovered; robots.txt is not linked.

title: jq: inspect a saved ffuf report
explanation: Local parsing lets you review evidence without sending more requests.
options: Run the structured ffuf example first. Keep the original report; this projection intentionally omits other fields.
result: URL, HTTP status and length for each recorded result.

title: Gobuster: choose the correct mode
explanation: DNS discovery asks a resolver about candidate names; virtual-host discovery varies HTTP host routing.
options: These are different from directory discovery and from Subfinder passive sources. Wildcard DNS and default virtual hosts create false positives. Do not assume each answer identifies a distinct application.
result: Installed mode-specific options without scanning a domain.

title: Wappalyzer: validate a version claim
command:
Record the detected product and any reported version.
Find a second independent signal.
Ask the application owner to verify the deployed build.
Record confidence and observation time.
explanation: A framework label or old banner is not proof of a vulnerable installation.
options: A reverse proxy, cached asset or customized header can mislead identification. Missing detections do not prove absence. Online lookup and API capabilities differ from the extension and may involve a crawl.
result: An inventory entry with evidence and uncertainty.

title: Review names before active probing
explanation: Keep passive discovery separate from an active test target list.
options: Confirm each candidate against scope and owner inventory. Shared services, stale names and third-party delegations need review. Do not pipe an unreviewed list straight into scanners.
result: A deduplicated candidate list; q exits less.

title: ffuf: preserve structured results
explanation: A structured report supports repeatable comparisons.
options: Save the wordlist, version, scope and filter settings alongside it. The same response length across two pages does not establish identical content.
result: A JSON report, replacing the named report if present.

title: Nuclei: inspect before choosing templates
explanation: Nuclei runs template-defined checks; the selected template determines requests and effects.
options: Read a template before running it: target paths, methods, payloads, matchers and callbacks. For this static lab choose a reviewed local informational template if available, not an entire template collection.
result: Help and a checklist for selecting a bounded check.

title: sqlmap: understand detection scope
explanation: sqlmap automates SQL injection testing. Its advanced options include operations far beyond detecting a suspected issue.
options: Learn only in an intentionally vulnerable isolated application with synthetic data. Fix the parameter, request, account and request budget first. The static Python server has no SQL backend and cannot demonstrate SQL injection.
result: Basic and extended help; no target requests.

title: Prepare and run the web-testing programs
explanation: First copy examples/web-programs from the Windows handbook folder into this Kali directory using your configured file-transfer method.
options: The supplied scripts use only built-in Python and Node libraries. Use Python 3.10+ and a supported Node version with ES modules. Keep the server in Terminal A; run the remaining examples in Terminal B.
result: A fictional local web app; a host Windows path is not automatically a Kali path.

title: JavaScript: inventory links and forms without submitting
explanation: Inspect the DOM of your own training page. No destination is fetched and no form is submitted.
options: Run in Developer Tools on the local fixture page, not in Node. It reports destinations and field names/types, omitting query strings, fragments and field values. This is a current-DOM snapshot, not a full crawler.
result: Link/form inventory. Paths and names may still be sensitive; a hidden token field does not prove that the server verifies it.

title: Python: start a synthetic web-testing fixture
explanation: A self-contained loopback server with predictable headers, cookie attributes, CORS responses, a redirect and a form. All cookies and content are fictional.
options: Save as fixture_server.py. Run python3 fixture_server.py --port 8891. It binds only 127.0.0.1. This is an HTTP fixture; the Secure cookie illustrates a response attribute, not proof a browser will accept it over this transport.
result: A local service for the following exercises. Ctrl+C stops it. The form has no implemented submission handler.

title: Compare response-header observations in both languages
command:
python3 web_review.py headers http://127.0.0.1:8891/strong
node web_review.mjs headers http://127.0.0.1:8891/strong
explanation: Run from the directory containing the scripts with the fixture server active.
options: The fixture sends CSP, nosniff and Referrer-Policy. It does not send HSTS or X-Frame-Options; frame-ancestors is supplied through CSP. Presence checks do not validate policy contents.
result: Equivalent JSON showing three present and two absent headers.

title: Review cookie attributes without exposing their values
command:
python3 web_review.py cookies http://127.0.0.1:8891/strong
node web_review.mjs cookies http://127.0.0.1:8891/weak
explanation: Compare the synthetic session and preference cookies.
options: The session fixture includes Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax. The preference fixture does not. Attribute requirements depend on cookie purpose and transport; the simple parser is not a full browser acceptance engine.
result: Cookie names and attributes, with no FAKE_ONLY values in the reports.

title: Observe a controlled CORS reflection
command:
python3 web_review.py cors http://127.0.0.1:8891/cors
node web_review.mjs cors http://127.0.0.1:8891/cors
explanation: Send the synthetic Origin https://review.invalid to the localhost fixture. No connection is made to that origin.
options: The fixture reflects the value and allows credentials, producing review_reflection true. The scripts do not send credentials, emulate browser cookie rules, perform a preflight or prove sensitive-data access.
result: A repeatable configuration observation requiring browser/context validation.

title: Compare authorization evidence and an ambiguous login page
command:
python3 response_diff.py baseline.json denied.json
node response_diff.mjs baseline.json denied.json
python3 response_diff.py baseline.json ambiguous.json
explanation: Use the supplied fictional evidence files. Baseline represents an owner response; denied is 403; ambiguous is a 200 login page.
options: The first comparison has different status and body. The ambiguous case has the same status but different body. Real access-control evidence also needs the authenticated identity and expected permission decision.
result: A demonstration of why status alone does not establish authorization.

title: Confirm redirects stay within the request budget
command:
python3 web_review.py headers http://127.0.0.1:8891/redirect
node web_review.mjs headers http://127.0.0.1:8891/redirect
explanation: Observe the redirect response itself.
options: Each tool makes one request and does not request /strong automatically. HTTP error statuses likewise remain observations when the response is readable; connection, parsing and size errors fail.

title: Python: HTTP headers, cookies and CORS reviewer
explanation: A complete program with three review modes. Each invocation sends one GET to the explicitly supplied HTTP(S) URL, keeps certificate validation enabled and does not follow redirects.
options: Save as web_review.py. Modes: headers, cookies, cors. Bodies over 256 KiB fail; output omits bodies and cookie values. No login is performed. Python uses a three-second blocking socket timeout, not an overall wall-clock deadline.
result: JSON observations or nonzero failure. CORS reflection and missing headers are review leads, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

title: JavaScript: HTTP headers, cookies and CORS reviewer
explanation: A complete program with three review modes. Each invocation sends one GET to the explicitly supplied HTTP(S) URL, keeps certificate validation enabled and does not follow redirects.
options: Save as web_review.mjs. Modes: headers, cookies, cors. Bodies over 256 KiB fail; output omits bodies and cookie values. No login is performed. Node uses a three-second request deadline and a 16 KiB response-header limit.
result: JSON observations or nonzero failure. CORS reflection and missing headers are review leads, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

title: Python: compare two response evidence files
explanation: Compare saved JSON response evidence without making network requests. Each input must contain an integer HTTP status and a body string.
options: Save as response_diff.py. Read at most 1 MiB per input. Output contains status/body equality, UTF-8 sizes and SHA-256 digests, not response contents. Store the original files securely; this custom JSON format is not HAR.
result: An evidence comparison. Different results can reflect login pages, timestamps or errors; confirm the expected role/object policy.

title: JavaScript: compare two response evidence files
explanation: Compare saved JSON response evidence without making network requests. Each input must contain an integer HTTP status and a body string.
options: Save as response_diff.mjs. Read at most 1 MiB per input. Output contains status/body equality, UTF-8 sizes and SHA-256 digests, not response contents. Store the original files securely; this custom JSON format is not HAR.
result: An evidence comparison. Different results can reflect login pages, timestamps or errors; confirm the expected role/object policy.

title: Security misconfiguration and exposed secrets
command: A production-like lab returns verbose debug information containing a synthetic secret.
explanation: Deployment settings expose capabilities, files or credentials beyond intended users.
impact_detail: Internal details, credentials or administrative access may be exposed.
lab_check: Review configuration and known routes in an owned environment using fake secrets. Inspect responses and storage permissions.
options: Disable debug features, remove unused endpoints, apply least privilege and store secrets outside public assets. Rotate any genuinely exposed credential.
result: Sensitive details are absent and credentials/configuration are corrected without breaking required functionality.
pitfall: Deleting a leaked file does not revoke a secret that was already exposed.

title: Clickjacking and UI redressing
command: An isolated test page embeds a training approval form in an unintended frame.
explanation: A sensitive interface can be framed or overlaid so a user interacts without understanding the actual target.
impact_detail: Unwanted user-authorized actions where the interaction remains possible.
lab_check: Use a harmless local framing exercise and verify the browser actual framing behavior.
options: Set suitable CSP frame-ancestors and compatible X-Frame-Options where needed. Require clear confirmation for consequential actions.
result: Untrusted framing is blocked while approved embedding works.
pitfall: Missing a header is not always exploitable; actual interaction and alternative protections matter.

title: Open redirects and host-header trust
command: A training reset link uses a request-provided hostname instead of the configured application origin.
explanation: The application uses an untrusted destination or host value when constructing trusted navigation or security links.
impact_detail: Misleading navigation or disclosure of security links in affected flows.
lab_check: Inspect generated links using synthetic data and controlled lab destinations.
options: Use configured trusted origins, allowlist required destinations and validate proxy-forwarded host data only from trusted infrastructure.
result: Untrusted hosts and destinations cannot influence sensitive links; valid navigation remains correct.
pitfall: A redirect feature is not automatically a security issue; evaluate where trust or sensitive data is involved.

title: Vulnerable components and software supply chain
command: A reachable dependency contains a confirmed flaw in the deployed build, or a release artifact is replaced outside the trusted process.
explanation: Dependencies, build inputs or delivered assets introduce weaknesses or unauthorized changes into the application.
impact_detail: Impact ranges from data exposure to compromise of application execution.
lab_check: Inventory exact deployed versions and dependency paths; verify applicability and artifact provenance without assuming every advisory affects the app.
options: Maintain dependencies, review advisories, protect build credentials and artifact integrity, and remove unused components.
result: The affected version or behavior is gone and the build/deployment path enforces expected provenance.
pitfall: A version match is a lead; backports, configuration and reachability affect the finding.

title: Cryptographic and password-storage failures
command: A lab stores recoverable plaintext passwords or logs an authentication token.
explanation: Sensitive information lacks suitable transport/storage protection, or secrets and keys are handled insecurely.
impact_detail: Disclosure can turn a database, log or network exposure into account compromise.
lab_check: Inspect the actual storage and transport design using synthetic credentials; check key access and rotation practices.
options: Use suitable password-hashing functions, maintained cryptographic libraries, validated TLS and managed key lifecycles. Minimize retained sensitive data.
result: Stored passwords are not recoverable plaintext, sensitive logs are removed and authorized functionality remains available.
pitfall: Hashing, encryption and encoding solve different problems; using a strong algorithm does not fix exposed keys.

title: Resource limits, errors and fail-open behavior
command: A training service grants access when its permission dependency returns an error.
explanation: Expensive work lacks bounds, or exceptional conditions cause security checks to permit access unexpectedly.
impact_detail: Availability loss or unauthorized access during failure conditions.
lab_check: Use fault injection and deliberately small bounded workloads in a test environment; observe decisions and cleanup.
options: Set request/time/size budgets, fail safely for security decisions, handle exceptions consistently and release resources correctly.
result: Dependency failures deny protected actions appropriately; legitimate recovery and normal requests still work.
pitfall: Do not load-test production merely to demonstrate a missing limit. Generic error messages alone do not enforce secure behavior.

title: Logging and alerting gaps
command: An unauthorized synthetic export attempt leaves no useful audit trail or owner notification.
explanation: Important security events are absent, unusable or never acted upon, delaying detection and response.
impact_detail: An incident can persist longer and be harder to investigate.
lab_check: Generate one controlled security event and trace it through application logging, collection and response workflow.
options: Record useful identity/action/result context without raw secrets; protect log integrity and access, define retention and test alert ownership.
result: The event is searchable and routed appropriately, without token leakage or duplicate noise.
pitfall: Missing logging usually amplifies another problem; it is not by itself proof of an exploitable entry point.

title: Mass assignment and API property authorization
command: A profile update accepts an internal approval flag from a basic training account.
explanation: Request fields are automatically bound to internal object properties that the caller must not control.
impact_detail: Unauthorized privilege or workflow changes.
lab_check: Use a disposable account and synthetic objects; compare documented writable fields against actual server updates.
options: Explicitly allowlist writable properties per operation and role; separate input models from database entities.
result: Forbidden properties are rejected or safely ignored and cannot change server state; allowed edits succeed.
pitfall: Filtering fields only in the browser does not protect an API request.

title: Business logic flaws
command: A synthetic coupon remains usable after its allowed redemption has completed.
explanation: Individual requests are valid but their combination violates the product rules.
impact_detail: Financial loss, workflow abuse or inconsistent records.
lab_check: Write the invariant and state transitions first; test a small number of reversible synthetic transactions.
options: Enforce invariants on the server, compute trusted prices there and validate workflow transitions at each step.
result: Invalid sequences fail while valid purchases, cancellations or redemptions remain correct.
pitfall: A scanner cannot infer every business rule from endpoint syntax.

title: Race conditions and duplicate processing
command: Two synthetic redemption requests both observe the same unused voucher.
explanation: Concurrent operations check and update shared state without sufficient atomicity or idempotency.
impact_detail: Double spending, duplicate actions or broken limits.
lab_check: Use an isolated app, synthetic state and a small controlled concurrent test; inspect final stored state, not only response codes.
options: Use transactions, atomic updates or appropriate locking; design idempotency keys and uniqueness constraints for the actual operation.
result: Concurrent and retried operations preserve the invariant; a legitimate single operation still succeeds.
pitfall: A race may not reproduce sequentially. A timed-out request may already have completed server-side.

title: Cache poisoning and cache deception
command: An isolated cache serves the wrong synthetic user representation after a request variation.
explanation: Poisoning stores an unintended attacker-influenced response for later users. Deception causes private content to be cached under a location treated as public.
impact_detail: Cross-user misinformation or disclosure of private content.
lab_check: Use a dedicated cache with synthetic accounts; record cache keys, response headers and hit/miss behavior.
options: Align cache keys with response variation, keep private responses out of shared caching and make routing/cache normalization consistent.
result: Users receive correct representations across cold and warm caches; private responses are not reused publicly.
pitfall: A cache header alone does not prove another user can receive the affected content.

title: HTTP request smuggling and desynchronization
command: A dedicated proxy/backend lab disagrees on where one synthetic request ends.
explanation: HTTP components disagree about message boundaries or translation, causing them to interpret a connection differently.
impact_detail: Request confusion, security-control bypass or cross-user effects depending on architecture.
lab_check: Study only in an isolated multi-component lab and correlate both sides of the proxy. Preserve raw messages and protocol versions.
options: Use consistent strict parsers, reject ambiguous requests, update intermediaries and validate protocol translation behavior.
result: Ambiguous traffic is rejected consistently without affecting subsequent normal requests.
pitfall: A timeout alone is weak evidence; tests can affect other traffic on shared connections.

title: JavaScript prototype pollution
command: A lab merge function changes a default property used by unrelated objects.
explanation: Untrusted property assignment alters inherited object behavior rather than only the intended data object.
impact_detail: Application behavior changes; further impact depends on a reachable code path that trusts the polluted property.
lab_check: Review unsafe merge/set paths with benign fixture properties and inspect object inheritance in a dedicated lab.
options: Use safer containers and merge logic, restrict keys and use own-property checks where appropriate. Maintain affected dependencies.
result: Untrusted input cannot alter shared prototypes and normal object updates remain correct.
pitfall: A pollution source alone does not prove a useful execution or authorization consequence.

title: WebSocket and GraphQL authorization
command: A training subscriber receives another test tenant event after changing a message parameter.
explanation: A connection or endpoint is authenticated once but individual messages, operations or fields lack adequate permission checks.
impact_detail: Unauthorized data access or actions beyond the connection intended privileges.
lab_check: Use test identities to compare permitted and prohibited messages/fields; inspect origin handling and session expiry.
options: Authorize each relevant operation, validate schemas, recheck session validity and bound message size or query complexity.
result: Unauthorized events/fields are blocked and normal subscriptions or queries continue.
pitfall: A single GraphQL URL or established WebSocket connection does not imply a single permission decision.

title: Feroxbuster: bounded content discovery
explanation: Discover candidate paths using the small site and wordlist from Lab 13.
options: Recursion and link extraction are disabled; one thread, a per-directory rate cap and a time limit constrain work. Review configuration files for additional enabled behavior.
result: Known paths and negative responses to interpret; no vulnerability verdict.

title: Feroxbuster: understand recursive growth
explanation: Recursion searches below discovered paths; extraction adds candidates found in responses.
options: Depth, extension expansion and multiple directories multiply requests. A per-directory rate limit is not necessarily a global limit. Preview the scope and use the preceding small lab before enabling recursion.
result: Installed flags and a basis for estimating request volume.

title: Arjun: test a tiny parameter dictionary
explanation: Arjun compares responses while trying candidate HTTP parameter names. Use the Chapter 30 fixture first.
options: Copy the supplied parameters.txt into the shown folder. The fixture ignores these parameters, so no meaningful discovery is expected. Calibration can send more requests than the number of words.
result: A controlled negative example; confirm a candidate manually before trusting it.

title: Param Miner: investigate one request
command:
Install Param Miner from the Burp extension catalog.
Select one in-scope training request.
Review extension settings and choose the relevant parameter or header discovery action.
Compare any candidate against a clean request in Repeater.
explanation: Param Miner helps identify inputs that influence responses but are not obvious in the captured request.
options: Use a dedicated training endpoint with no shared cache users. Generated requests can be numerous. A changed response can reflect a cache, randomness or error handling rather than a meaningful parameter.
result: A candidate input with baseline evidence.

title: Autorize: compare two test identities
command:
Prepare privileged and lower-privilege lab accounts.
Configure the lower-privilege session in Autorize.
Restrict scope to one harmless read endpoint.
Capture the privileged request and inspect the repeated lower-privilege response.
explanation: Autorize automates authorization comparisons using alternative session information.
options: Inspect all generated requests. Remove stale authentication headers and verify the actual identity. Avoid replaying purchases, deletes or other state-changing operations as a first exercise.
result: A comparison requiring body/permission review, not merely matching lengths.

title: JWT Editor: inspect a synthetic token
command:
Use a disposable token from your own training issuer.
Open its JWT Editor view.
Inspect claims and algorithm metadata.
Verify it with the known test key.
Compare rejection of a modified token with acceptance of the original.
explanation: JWT Editor assists with structured token inspection and cryptographic operations.
options: Decoding is not verification. Use only synthetic keys and tokens. Expected issuer, audience and time checks belong to application validation in addition to signature checking.
result: Evidence that your training application handles valid and invalid tokens correctly.

title: Dalfox: plan context-aware XSS checks
explanation: Dalfox focuses on XSS discovery and validation workflows.
options: Start with a deliberately vulnerable XSS lab and one known parameter. Review request/worker limits, mining and browser verification options for your installed version. Avoid enabling external callbacks without accounting for their data handling.
result: A scoped test plan; reflection alone is not executable XSS.

title: Dalfox: validate the finding manually
command:
Record the parameter and reflection context.
Compare the unchanged request and reported test case.
Check browser behavior in the dedicated lab.
Identify the unsafe rendering operation and verify the fix.
explanation: An automated XSS lead becomes useful when connected to actual browser interpretation.
options: Distinguish HTML text, attributes, script contexts and DOM processing. Do not classify every reflected marker as exploitable. Retest the correct output encoding or safe rendering API.
result: A reproducible finding with a specific remediation.

title: mitmproxy: inspect an explicitly proxied local request
explanation: Start an interactive proxy on a separate port from Burp.
options: Keep it in Terminal A. Route only your lab client through it. HTTPS interception needs a trusted test CA in the lab client; the HTTP example needs no CA installation. q opens quit controls.
result: A local proxy ready to show selected traffic.

title: mitmproxy: send one request through the proxy
explanation: Send one fixture request through the preceding proxy.
options: Start the Chapter 30 fixture first. --noproxy with an empty value prevents environment proxy-bypass settings from skipping the local proxy. Inspect headers and body in mitmproxy.
result: A visible HTTP flow and the fictional response.

title: testssl.sh: inspect a configured TLS service
explanation: Assess supported TLS protocol versions on a separately configured owned HTTPS service.
options: The lab name must resolve to your test service. Check the installed executable name/path. Protocol selection still involves multiple handshakes; this does not exercise the plain HTTP fixtures.
result: A protocol-support report; compare it with your required policy.

title: ZAP Automation Framework: make a repeatable plan
command:
Define an exact context and starting URL.
Configure a dedicated test user if authentication is required.
Start with requestor/passive-analysis jobs and explicit success checks.
Review the YAML plan before adding spider or active-scan jobs.
explanation: The Automation Framework describes ordered assessment jobs and their configuration.
options: Set limits and authentication verification rather than assuming the scanner stayed logged in. Passive analysis evaluates traffic; crawlers and active jobs generate traffic and may trigger application actions.
result: A versioned plan with documented coverage and failure conditions.

title: Schemathesis: understand schema-driven API testing
explanation: Schemathesis generates tests from API schemas and checks behavior against expectations.
options: Use a disposable API with synthetic data. Generated cases may call POST, PUT or DELETE; restrict operations and case counts before running. A schema cannot express all object permissions and business rules.
result: Installed options for selecting schema, endpoint scope and test limits.

title: Schemathesis: triage a failing case
command:
Preserve the generated request and application build.
Reproduce once against reset synthetic state.
Decide whether the schema, application or test assumption is wrong.
Add a regression case and retest.
explanation: A failure can indicate contract drift, missing validation or a deeper application weakness.
options: Do not assign vulnerability severity just because an unexpected response occurred. Review data exposure, authorization and business impact separately.
result: A minimal, classified, repeatable API failure.

title: Nuclei: inspect the supplied informational template
command:
id: fieldbook-local-header
info:
  name: Fieldbook local nosniff observation
  author: fieldbook
  severity: info
http:
  - method: GET
    path:
      - "{{BaseURL}}/strong"
    redirects: false
    matchers:
      - type: word
        part: header
        words:
          - "X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff"
        case-insensitive: true
explanation: This template observes a known fixture header; a match reports a condition, not a vulnerability.
options: Save as local-header.yaml. It defines one GET path and no redirect following, fuzzing, code execution or external callback. Review every template before use, including downloaded ones.

title: Nuclei: validate and run one reviewed template
explanation: Run from the copied advanced-web folder with the Chapter 30 fixture active.
options: -validate checks template structure; -rl and -c limit rate/concurrency. -ni disables Interactsh and -duc disables update checks. Check installed help if flags differ; do not replace the selected template with an entire collection.
result: An informational header match at /strong; no evidence of an exploit.

title: Semgrep: inspect a small local source rule
command:
rules:
  - id: fieldbook-python-eval
    languages: [python]
    message: Review dynamic eval; prefer a constrained parser for untrusted data.
    severity: WARNING
    pattern: eval($EXPR)
explanation: A Semgrep pattern identifies a Python syntax shape worth reviewing.
options: Save as review-eval.yaml. This simple rule flags eval calls regardless of whether the input is controlled by a user. It does not establish data flow or exploitability.

title: Semgrep: analyze the supplied synthetic file
explanation: Run a local rule against a deliberately inert teaching file. Do not execute the sample function.
options: Copy examples/advanced-web into Kali first. The scan parses code; it does not run the application. Review findings in context and distinguish detection from a confirmed reachable flaw.
result: One expected eval finding; normal default scan exit behavior may not treat findings as errors.

title: Gitleaks: review a trusted source directory
explanation: Scan a local source directory for secret-like patterns.
options: Directory mode does not review complete Git history. --redact reduces secret exposure in output; reports can still contain sensitive metadata. A match needs validation and any real exposed credential needs rotation.
result: A redacted report; the supplied fixtures intentionally contain no real credentials.

title: pip-audit: inspect Python dependency advisories
explanation: Run against a trusted requirements file in a dedicated project environment.
options: Audit services receive package/version information. Resolution can involve package metadata/build tooling, so treat unfamiliar requirements as untrusted. An advisory match needs version, deployment and reachability review.
result: Known dependency advisories or a no-known-findings result; not a complete application assessment.

title: npm audit: review JavaScript dependencies
explanation: Run in a trusted Node project with its manifest and lockfile.
options: Dependency data is sent to the configured registry. Review production versus development paths. This command reports; do not blindly apply audit fix or force upgrades without compatibility testing.
result: JSON advisories or audit errors; nonzero exit can indicate findings.

title: Combine dynamic, static and dependency evidence
command:
Record the endpoint and its observed behavior.
Locate the responsible source path, if available.
Check deployed dependency versions and configuration.
Reproduce with synthetic data.
Fix the root cause and retest the original case plus an allowed case.
explanation: Different tools observe different parts of the same application.
options: Keep scanner version, rule/template version, identity and scope with the evidence. Avoid counting the same root cause repeatedly just because multiple tools report it.
result: One actionable finding with corroborating evidence and explicit coverage limits.

title: Lynis local audit
explanation: Audit this Kali system for configuration weaknesses and hardening opportunities.
options: Install lynis if absent. Read recommendations in context; a warning is not proof of compromise.
result: An audit summary and report paths.

title: Open Burp Suite
explanation: Launch the graphical web security workbench.
options: Use a temporary project and its built-in browser for your local lab. Interception can pause browser requests until forwarded.

title: Open OWASP ZAP
explanation: Launch a graphical web proxy and assessment tool if installed.
options: Keep targets within an approved lab. Active scans send test requests and may change application data.

title: Inspect Nikto options
explanation: Read the local web-server scanner's available settings.
options: Check scope and output options before testing an application.

title: Scan the local training server
explanation: Send web checks to the Python server created in this book.
options: Results can be noisy. A generic Python server is not a production security benchmark. Stop with Ctrl+C if needed.

title: Gobuster directory help
explanation: Learn the directory enumeration mode without sending requests.
options: A real run needs an authorized URL and a carefully sized wordlist.

title: SQLmap overview
explanation: Display help for the SQL injection testing tool.
options: Use an intentionally vulnerable, owned web lab before attempting testing; automated tests can alter data.

title: Open Metasploit console
explanation: Open the framework console without selecting or running an exploit.
options: At its prompt, help lists console commands, version shows versions, and exit leaves.

title: Hashcat device inventory
explanation: List available compute backends and devices for offline password auditing.
options: VirtualBox usually does not expose your host GPU as a native cracking device. This command performs no cracking.

title: John supported formats
explanation: List hash formats supported by your installed John build.
options: Listing formats does not test passwords. Only audit hashes you are authorized to possess.

title: DNS: query an owned lab resolver
explanation: Ask an explicitly configured lab DNS server about an example training zone.
options: Replace server and zone with your setup. A is an IPv4 record query. Inspect status and answer/authority sections; NXDOMAIN differs from timeout and from an empty successful answer.
result: A DNS response or bounded diagnostic.

title: DNS: compare TCP transport
explanation: Check the same question over TCP when diagnosing DNS transport behavior.
options: DNS needs more than UDP-only assumptions. Compare the same resolver and name. A transport difference may be caused by firewall policy rather than zone contents.

title: SMB: list shares with a test identity
explanation: Request a share list on a configured owned Samba or Windows lab server.
options: Enter the password at the prompt, not on the command line. A listed share is not proof of read or write access. Use the account and domain format required by your lab.
result: Shares allowed to be listed, or an authentication diagnostic.

title: SNMP: read one object in a configured lab
